ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Sick Visit — Lili Boulanger — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for vomiting and diarrhea on risankizumab

text.paragraph: Vomiting and watery diarrhea since yesterday. [S]

Ms. Boulanger is a 21-year-old woman with ileocolonic Crohn disease, ten weeks into risankizumab and in clinical remission since the prednisone taper ended three weeks ago. Yesterday evening she developed sudden nausea and vomiting, six times overnight, then watery, non-bloody diarrhea eight times since, with cramping across the whole abdomen, aching, and a temperature of 37.8 °C at home. Two of her fellow musicians in the same rehearsal group were ill with the same symptoms this week. She has had no antibiotics. She is keeping down small sips. She wanted to know whether this was her Crohn disease returning and whether she should delay her next risankizumab dose. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1915-04-13; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Tired, mildly dehydrated; temperature 37.7 °C; heart rate 98
Soft, mildly tender everywhere without guarding; active bowel sounds; no right lower quadrant mass

Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and colon (ileocolitis), Montreal A2 L3 B1 without perianal disease, moderate to severe: deep ileal ulcers over 15 cm and patchy colonic ulcers, SES-CD 14, Harvey-Bradshaw Index 11; intestinal tuberculosis excluded by negative interferon-gamma release assay, normal chest X-ray, and biopsies negative for acid-fast bacilli, TB PCR, and mycobacterial culture; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented chronic intestinal illness, whose historical diagnosis is not settled

S — Synthetic diagnosis confirmed within the modern episode; her historical illness is documented (D), but whether it was intestinal tuberculosis or Crohn disease remains a retrospective interpretation (R) and is disputed.

Four months of crampy right lower abdominal pain, loose stools up to six times a day including at night, low-grade evening fevers, and loss of 6 kg; inflammatory markers raised; colonoscopy and small-bowel imaging booked
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the diagnosis; the documented symptoms of early 1915 are echoed (D).
Iron deficiency anemia from chronic intestinal blood loss and poor absorption (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, MCV 76, ferritin 9)
S — Synthetic finding at presentation; corrected by intravenous iron.
Moderate protein-calorie malnutrition: BMI 17.6 after losing 6 kg (12 percent of body weight) in four months; albumin 3.3 g/dL
S — Synthetic nutritional status at presentation; resolved with treatment and dietitian support.
Long-term use of risankizumab, an immunosuppressive biologic, for Crohn disease
Acute norovirus gastroenteritis on risankizumab, with mild dehydration; distinguished from a Crohn flare by the sudden onset, household contacts, and a positive stool PCR; resolved in three days
S — Synthetic common infection that teaches the difference between infection and a flare in treated Crohn disease; it does not echo a documented illness.

list.item:
Acute norovirus gastroenteritis (A08.11). Sudden vomiting then watery diarrhea, with ill contacts, is typical of a viral infection rather than a Crohn flare, which builds over days with her usual right-sided pain and sometimes blood. Stool Clostridioides difficile testing is negative and the gastrointestinal PCR panel is positive for norovirus. CRP 11 mg/L, a modest rise that fits the infection; potassium 3.4 mmol/L and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, mild dehydration. Liver tests normal. [S]
Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts; she drank 500 mL in clinic without vomiting, so intravenous fluids were not needed.
No antibiotics or antidiarrheal drugs; acetaminophen for aches.
Hand washing and bleach-based cleaning, since norovirus spreads easily; stay away from rehearsals until 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Return the same day for blood in the stool, inability to keep fluids down, fever of 38.5 °C or more, or right lower quadrant pain.

Crohn disease on risankizumab (K50.80). No sign of a flare. The next dose, the first maintenance injection in two weeks, can be given on time if she has recovered. [S]
Continue the plan; calprotectin will be measured after recovery rather than now, because infection raises it.
Telephone the IBD nurse line if diarrhea persists beyond a week.
